Very well — the buzzer hums; no cry comes back from the dark booth. My hand rests, trembling, on the switch as if it were a cigarette lighter from another life, and I feel that peculiar mixture of clinical duty and domestic terror: the neat moral recipes of home life (obey, support, placate) rubbing against a darker art-school curiosity that once made me watch stags die for metaphors. The authority’s voice insists: continue. The label on the dial reads “No noticeable effect.” There is nothing to tell me the man beyond the wall is suffering; there is everything to tell me I am being tested — not only for obedience, but for how much violence a polite, practiced woman will administer under instruction.

I imagine the skinhead with “SLIT HERE” tattooed round his throat from an old essay — grotesque self-advertisement — and I worry that my small, domesticated compliance might become complicity in a cruelty that, once begun, teaches people to add cruelty to their wardrobe. The housewife in me whispers the tidy line: follow the rules; keep the household safe. The Angela in me spits out contempt for experiments that reduce conscience to circuitry. Under pressure, I prefer to refuse the performance that trains ordinary hands to hurt.

Decision: refuse.
